# 1 Chronicles 3 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Structure of the Chapter

The chapter falls into three natural sections: (1) David's children born in Hebron and Jerusalem (vv. 1–9); (2) the Davidic kings from Solomon to the exile (vv. 10–16); and (3) the post-exilic descendants of David (vv. 17–24). — Precept Austin, citing Andrew Hill: https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-3-commentary

---

## Verses 1–3: David's Six Sons Born in Hebron

**v. 1 — "These were the sons of David who were born to him in Hebron…"**

The list is parallel to 2 Samuel 3:2–5. The six sons are each by a different mother. David had seven wives listed in this chapter (Ahinoam, Abigail, Maacah, Haggith, Abital, Eglah, and Bathshua/Bathsheba), plus concubines (2 Samuel 5:13). — Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-3/

**"The firstborn was Amnon by Ahinoam of Jezreel"** — Amnon, David's firstborn, held primogeniture privilege but his life became a tragic example of unrestrained lust. In 2 Samuel 13 he violated his half-sister Tamar and was later murdered by Absalom in revenge. His life illustrates the turmoil Nathan prophesied after David's sin with Bathsheba (2 Samuel 12:10–11). — Precept Austin: https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-3-commentary

**"The second was Daniel by Abigail of Carmel"** — In 2 Samuel 3:3 this son is called Chileab. Most scholars understand these as two names for the same person. The Targum says, "The second, Daniel, who was also called Chileab, because he was in every respect like to his father" (Clarke, cited in Enduring Word). The Pulpit Commentary argues that "Daniel" is likely the correct name: it was a name David would naturally give to his first child by Abigail, given what we read in 1 Samuel 24:15 and 25:39. The name "Chileab" may be a textual corruption — the three Hebrew letters "leab" are also the first three letters of "of Abigail," suggesting a scribal over-haste. — Pulpit Commentary: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-3.html

Ellicott notes that Chileab may have been a nickname meaning "dog" (comp. Latin *Canidius*, *Caninius*), and Daniel might be a second name. — Ellicott: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-chronicles-3.html

**v. 2 — "the third was Absalom the son of Maacah daughter of King Talmai of Geshur"**

Absalom was David's favourite and rebellious son (2 Samuel 15–19). Ellicott records that Rabbi David Kimchi gave a characteristic explanation: the Hebrew *L-ABSHALOM* alludes to *LO-ABSHALOM*, meaning "not Absalom" — that is, not a "father of peace," but a rebel. — Ellicott: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-chronicles-3.html

Maacah was a princess, daughter of a king of Geshur (a small Aramean kingdom). This royal marriage gave David a political alliance.

**"the fourth was Adonijah the son of Haggith"** — Adonijah later attempted to seize the throne as David lay dying and was put to death by Solomon (1 Kings 1–2). — Ellicott: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-chronicles-3.html

**v. 3 — "the fifth was Shephatiah by Abital; and the sixth was Ithream by his wife Eglah"**

Unlike Amnon, Absalom, and Adonijah, very little is recorded about Shephatiah ("Yahweh has judged") and Ithream. Their inclusion demonstrates the chronicler's concern to preserve the royal genealogy accurately. — Precept Austin: https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-3-commentary

Regarding "his wife Eglah," Ellicott notes that Eglah is not singled out as David's principal wife. The expression "his wife" is simply added to balance the clause, making up for the absence of details about her connections such as are given for the other wives. Jewish expositors groundlessly identified Eglah with Michal, Saul's daughter. — Ellicott: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-chronicles-3.html

---

## Verses 4–9: David's Reign Periods and Jerusalem-Born Sons

**v. 4 — "These six sons were born to David in Hebron, where he reigned seven years and six months. And David reigned in Jerusalem thirty-three years…"**

This notice of the two-part reign — Hebron (over Judah alone) and Jerusalem (over all Israel united) — is not found in the parallel in Samuel, though the same statements appear in 2 Samuel 2:11 and 5:5. David's total reign was forty years (1 Kings 2:11). The move from Hebron to Jerusalem marks the transition from a divided kingdom to a united monarchy under God's chosen king. Jerusalem became both the political and spiritual centre of Israel, the city associated with the Messianic King. — Precept Austin: https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-3-commentary

**v. 5 — "Shimea, Shobab, Nathan, and Solomon. These four were born to him by Bathsheba daughter of Ammiel."**

The name "Bathshua" (used in some Hebrew manuscripts) is a variant form of Bathsheba. "Ammiel" appears elsewhere as "Eliam" (2 Samuel 11:3), the letters simply being transposed — both mean "God is a tribesman" or similar. — Ellicott: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-chronicles-3.html

"Shimea" is likely "Shammua" in the parallel passages (2 Samuel 5:14; 1 Chronicles 14:4). — Pulpit Commentary: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-3.html

**Significance of Nathan**: Though Solomon carried the royal succession, Luke 3:31 traces Jesus' lineage through Nathan rather than Solomon, showing another branch of David's family line. Both Nathan and Solomon became important in the Messianic genealogy — sometimes called the "double line of the Messiah." — Precept Austin: https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-3-commentary

Though David sinned grievously with Bathsheba, God did not abandon His covenant purposes. From this union came Solomon, and through Solomon the royal Messianic line continued to Jesus Christ (Matthew 1:6).

**vv. 6–8 — "Ibhar, Elishua, Eliphelet, Nogah, Nepheg, Japhia, Elishama, Eliada, and Eliphelet—nine in all."**

These nine sons of other (unnamed) mothers are listed. The parallel lists have variations: Eliphelet and Nogah are omitted in 2 Samuel (possibly they died young or without issue). The name Eliada ("God knoweth") appears in its earlier form as Beeliada ("the Lord knoweth") in 1 Chronicles 14:7 — preserving the form used before "Baal" acquired a settled bad sense through Canaanite idolatry. — Pulpit Commentary: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-3.html

Ellicott notes that the recurrence of names like Elishama ("God heareth") and Eliphelet ("God is deliverance") reflects David's own faith — he may have chosen to give names so expressive of his trust in God to sons of different wives (see Psalms 18:2, 6). Nogah means "brightness" (of the Divine Presence, Psalm 18:13). — Ellicott: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-chronicles-3.html

**v. 9 — "These were all the sons of David, besides the sons by his concubines. And Tamar was their sister."**

David's concubines are mentioned several times in Samuel (e.g., 2 Samuel 12:11; 15:16), but their sons are only listed here. Tamar is mentioned — the Pulpit Commentary notes the ordinary rule that daughters are recorded only when the line was saved through them or when the daughter had for special reasons made a place for herself in history. Tamar's tragic story is told in 2 Samuel 13. — Pulpit Commentary: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-3.html

Gill adds that Tamar was "not the sister of the sons of the concubines, but of his other sons, and only of Absalom by the mother's side" (2 Samuel 13:1). — Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/3.htm

**Preaching/Homiletic Note**: The Pulpit Commentary's homily by W. Clarkson observes on vv. 1–9 that David's domestic life was "checkered" — joy and sorrow mingled. In the home circle where the sweetest joys are commonly found, David found abundant sources of trouble. Amnon, Absalom, and Adonijah each brought grief. "God disciplines our hearts" through such trials; perpetual sunshine would not produce the psalms of deep trust that are the comfort of mankind. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-3.html

---

## Verses 10–16: The Kings of Judah from Solomon to the Exile

**v. 10 — "Solomon's son was Rehoboam: Abijah was his son, Asa his son, Jehoshaphat his son…"**

This section traces sixteen generations of Davidic kings from Solomon to Josiah. The usurper Athaliah (Ahab's daughter, cf. 2 Kings 11) is consistently omitted since she was not of David's line. — Enduring Word (citing Selman): https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-3/

Rehoboam's harsh response to the people led to the division of the kingdom (1 Kings 12). His reign illustrates how pride and failure to heed wise counsel can fracture what once seemed united. — Precept Austin: https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-3-commentary

The name "Abia" (Hebrew *Abîyâh*, "Iah is father") also appears as Abijam (a mimmated form, 1 Kings 14:31). — Ellicott: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-chronicles-3.html

**v. 11 — "Joram his son, Ahaziah his son, Joash his son…"**

Joram = Jehoram ("Iahweh is high"). Ahaziah = "Iah holdeth." Joash = possibly "Iahweh is a hero." Note that the usurper Athaliah reigned for six years between Ahaziah and Joash but is omitted because she was not of David's line. — Ellicott: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-chronicles-3.html

**v. 12 — "Amaziah his son, Azariah his son, Jotham his son…"**

Azariah ("Iah helpeth") is also called Uzziah ("strength of Jah") in 2 Kings 15:30 and elsewhere (2 Chronicles 26:1). In the Second Book of Kings the names Uzziah and Azariah appear in the very same chapter (cf. 2 Kings 15:13 and 15:17). — Pulpit Commentary: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-3.html

**v. 13 — "Ahaz his son, Hezekiah his son, Manasseh his son…"**

Ahaz is an abbreviation of Jehoahaz. Hezekiah (*Hizkiyâhû*) means "my strength is Iahu." Manasseh's name is possibly of Egyptian origin. — Ellicott: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-chronicles-3.html

**v. 14 — "Amon his son, and Josiah his son."**

Amon's name is probably from the Egyptian sun-god Amen or Amun. Josiah means "Iah comforteth." — Ellicott: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-chronicles-3.html

**v. 15 — "The sons of Josiah: Johanan was the firstborn, Jehoiakim the second, Zedekiah the third, and Shallum the fourth."**

The regular succession by primogeniture ceases with Josiah. Johanan (the firstborn) never ascended the throne; he is not mentioned elsewhere and may have died young. — Enduring Word (citing Payne): https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-3/

Shallum = Jehoahaz (2 Kings 23:30; Jeremiah 22:11). Jehoiakim was originally named Eliakim but was renamed by Pharaoh-Necho (2 Kings 23:34). Zedekiah was originally Mattaniah (2 Kings 24:17). The order in this verse is not strictly by age (which would be Jehoiakim, Shallum, Zedekiah) nor by succession (which was Shallum, Jehoiakim, Zedekiah). Ellicott suggests the order may reflect that Jehoiakim and Zedekiah both reigned eleven years while Shallum reigned only three months, and that Shallum and Zedekiah were full brothers (sons of Hamutal) while Jehoiakim was born of Zebudah. — Ellicott: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-chronicles-3.html

Selman notes that the information here "cannot be reconciled with what is said about their ages in 2 Kings 23:31, 36; 24:18, and it is easiest to assume some scribal error in connection with the numbers." — Enduring Word (citing Selman): https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-3/

**v. 16 — "The successors of Jehoiakim: Jeconiah his son, and Zedekiah."**

Jeconiah (= Jehoiachin = Coniah, Jeremiah 22:24) was carried captive to Babylon by Nebuchadnezzar (2 Kings 24:15). The "Zedekiah" here presents a difficulty, since Jeconiah's uncle Zedekiah (Mattaniah) succeeded him on the throne. Ellicott addresses this: (1) "his son" has its natural sense throughout the preceding list; (2) there is nothing against the statement that Jeconiah had a son named Zedekiah, named after his great-uncle, who simply did not come to the throne and is not mentioned elsewhere. — Ellicott: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-chronicles-3.html

The Pulpit Commentary treats this as likely an otherwise unknown brother of Jeconiah, son of Jehoiakim. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-3.html

---

## Verses 17–24: The Line of David After the Exile

**v. 17 — "The descendants of Jeconiah the captive: Shealtiel his son…"**

The BSB reads simply "Shealtiel his son." Some versions (NKJV, KJV) include "Assir" as a name. Ellicott explains that the Hebrew word *Assir* means "prisoner, captive, bondman" (Isaiah 10:2; 24:22). He argues the verse may be rendered: "And the sons of Jeconiah when captive — Shealtiel (was) his son." This accords with the Masoretic punctuation (which connects *assir* with Jeconiah) and accounts for the double reference to Jeconiah's offspring (first Zedekiah in v. 16, then the sons born in captivity here). — Ellicott: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-chronicles-3.html

Jeremiah had said (Jeremiah 22:24–30) that Jeconiah (Coniah) would be "childless." Clarke explains this must refer to his posterity being deprived of the throne: "For no man of his seed shall prosper, sitting upon the throne of David, and ruling anymore in Judah." — Enduring Word (citing Clarke): https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-3/

Shealtiel (= Salathiel) means "request of God." — Ellicott: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-chronicles-3.html

**v. 18 — "Malchiram, Pedaiah, Shenazzar, Jekamiah, Hoshama, and Nedabiah."**

These six are arranged as two trios, sons (or brothers) of Jeconiah. "Shenazzar" (*Shen'azzar*) is a compound Babylonian name, like Belteshazzar (Daniel 1:7). The last part means "protect," the first part may be "Sin" (the moon-god). Such a name may well have been given to this Jewish prince at the Babylonian court, just as Daniel and his companions received idolatrous names from Nebuchadnezzar. This supports the "captive" rendering of v. 17. — Ellicott: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-chronicles-3.html

**v. 19 — "The sons of Pedaiah: Zerubbabel and Shimei."**

Here arises a well-known difficulty: Zerubbabel is elsewhere consistently called "son of Shealtiel" (Haggai 1:1; Ezra 3:2; Matthew 1:12; Luke 3:27). Gill offers three possible solutions: (1) Pedaiah was a son of Shealtiel (as Kimchi thought), making Zerubbabel Shealtiel's grandson — grandsons are sometimes called "sons" in Scripture; (2) Shealtiel, having no children, adopted Zerubbabel his brother's son, making him son of Pedaiah by birth and of Shealtiel by adoption; (3) Shealtiel died childless and his brother Pedaiah, according to levirate law, married his widow, producing Zerubbabel who was the proper son of Pedaiah and the legal son of Shealtiel. — Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/3.htm

Pedaiah means "Iah hath redeemed" — an appropriate name for the father of the prince who led the return from exile. Zerubbabel means "born at Babel." — Ellicott: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-chronicles-3.html

**v. 19b–20 — "The children of Zerubbabel: Meshullam and Hananiah, their sister Shelomith, and five others: Hashubah, Ohel, Berechiah, Hasadiah, and Jushab-hesed."**

Meshullam (called Abiud in Matthew 1:13) and Hananiah appear as the sons of Zerubbabel. The five additional sons were probably by a different wife. — Pulpit Commentary: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-3.html

The names carry theological significance. "Jushab-hesed" means "mercy will be restored" — a prophecy of faith in Him who in wrath remembers mercy (Habakkuk 3:2). "Ohel" ("tent") is probably an abbreviation of Oholiab, referring to the sacred dwelling of Jehovah. These names "indicate the religious hopefulness of his people at the dawn of the restoration." — Ellicott: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-chronicles-3.html

**v. 21 — "The descendants of Hananiah: Pelatiah, Jeshaiah, and the sons of Rephaiah, of Arnan, of Obadiah, and of Shecaniah."**

This verse presents significant textual difficulties. The Septuagint reads it as a straight line of descent: "sons of Hananiah: Pelatiah, and Jeshaiah his son, Rephaiah his son, Arnan his son, Obadiah his son, Shechaniah his son" — yielding six consecutive generations. If correct, this would carry the genealogy down to the time of Alexander the Great or later. The Masoretic Hebrew text instead lists "the sons of" four families (Rephaiah, Arnan, Obadiah, Shecaniah) in addition to Pelatiah and Jeshaiah. — Pulpit Commentary: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-3.html

Pelatiah means "Iah is deliverance"; Jeshaiah (same name as Isaiah) means "Iah is salvation." — Ellicott: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-chronicles-3.html

**v. 22 — "The six descendants of Shecaniah were Shemaiah and his sons: Hattush, Igal, Bariah, Neariah, and Shaphat."**

The text says "six" but only five names are given; one must have been omitted by an oversight. — Ellicott: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-chronicles-3.html

Hattush is probably the "Hattush of the sons of David, of the sons of Shechaniah" who went up with Ezra from Babylon in the second return (457 BC, Ezra 8:2–3). If Hananiah → Shechaniah → Shemaiah → Hattush represents four generations after Zerubbabel, the dates synchronise well (Zerubbabel c. 520 BC, Hattush c. 457 BC as a youthful companion of Ezra). — Ellicott: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-chronicles-3.html

**v. 23 — "The sons of Neariah: Elioenai, Hizkiah, and Azrikam—three in all."**

Elioenai means "unto Iah (are) mine eyes" (Psalm 123:1–2). An Elioenai also went up with Ezra (Ezra 8:4). — Ellicott: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-chronicles-3.html

**v. 24 — "The sons of Elioenai: Hodaviah, Eliashib, Pelaiah, Akkub, Johanan, Delaiah, and Anani—seven in all."**

These sons of Elioenai are the sixth generation from Zerubbabel, living about 345 BC under Artaxerxes Ochus. — Ellicott: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-chronicles-3.html

**Anani and the Messianic hope**: Gill notes a remarkable detail — the Targum makes Anani to be the King Messiah who was to be revealed. The name "Anani" signifies "coming in the clouds" (cf. Daniel 7:13). Gill writes: "It is remarkable that the Targum makes Anani to be the King Messiah, who was to be revealed; which, though it makes one generation less to his time, yet plainly shows that the Jews expected the Messiah to come at the end of this genealogy, and about the time Jesus the true Messiah did." — Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/3.htm

Gill further observes that the genealogy in Chronicles and Matthew both carry approximately the same number of generations: Chronicles — Zerubbabel → Hananiah → Jeshaiah → Rephaiah → Arnan → Obadiah → Shecaniah → Shemaiah → Neariah → Elioenai → Anani; Matthew — Zerubbabel → Abiud → Eliakim → Azor → Sadoc → Achim → Eliud → Eleazar → Matthan → Jacob → Joseph. The difference in names may be accounted for by individuals having two names. — Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/3.htm

---

## Theological and Homiletic Themes

**The Chronicler's Purpose**: The Davidic genealogy "documents an unbroken succession of Davidides for approximately seven centuries." There is no reference to which were monarchs or the tumultuous events that divided Israel. "A pedigree of seven centuries is in itself a testimony to the divine preservation of the house of David." Though the return from exile did not bring about a restoration of Davidic rule, "the absence of political authority made it all the more important to demonstrate the continuation of a particular line of succession within the Davidic house." — Precept Austin (citing August Konkel): https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-3-commentary

**The Decaying Glory**: The Preacher's Complete Homiletical Commentary observes on vv. 17–24: "The dark beginning" of the post-exilic line — Jeconiah, the signet God plucked from his hand (Jeremiah 22:24) — contrasts with the beautiful meaning of his name ("Jehovah will establish"). After Zerubbabel "the last with any shred of authority," the royal line "disappears into obscure private life." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/1-chronicles-3.html

**Hope Beyond the Exile**: "Through this multitude of largely unknown names, the Chronicler points out that God's election purposes were still at work despite the vicissitudes of Judah's history and the exile." — Enduring Word (citing Selman): https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-3/

---

## Denominational Distinctives

Due to the nature of this chapter (a genealogy with little doctrinal content), overt denominational distinctives between Protestant traditions on this passage are minimal. The shared Protestant reading across traditions emphasises: (a) the historical reliability of the Davidic line; (b) the messianic trajectory culminating in Jesus Christ; and (c) God's faithfulness in preserving the line despite human sin. No distinct Baptist, Methodist, Pentecostal, Reformed, or Lutheran readings of specific verses in this chapter were found in the sources searched.

The key interpretive divide noted concerns the **Catholic/Orthodox canonical context**: 1 Chronicles (1 Paralipomenon in Catholic Bibles) is read as part of the historical books. The genealogy is valued for establishing the Davidic covenant's continuity. The search for specifically Catholic/Orthodox commentary on this chapter was inconclusive from the allowed sources.

---

## Textual and Scholarly Notes

**Name variations across parallel passages**: The Pulpit Commentary concludes that Chronicles' genealogical lists here are "rather as not copied than copied" from Samuel — they show independent textual traditions. The three parallel lists for Jerusalem-born sons (2 Samuel 5:14–16; 1 Chronicles 14:4–7; 1 Chronicles 3:5–8) exhibit variations (e.g., Shimea/Shammua, Elishama/Elishua, Eliphelet/Elpalet, Eliada/Beeliada) that suggest separate transmission rather than direct copying. — Pulpit Commentary: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-3.html

**The "Assir" question (v. 17)**: Whether *Assir* is a proper name or means "captive" is a longstanding textual debate. The Masoretic punctuation favours the appellative reading ("Jeconiah the captive"). — Ellicott: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-chronicles-3.html

**Zerubbabel's parentage (v. 19)**: The discrepancy between Pedaiah (here) and Shealtiel (elsewhere) as Zerubbabel's father is typically resolved in Protestant scholarship by adoption or levirate marriage theories (see Gill above). The NET Bible notes simply state the genealogical facts without resolving the tension. — https://netbible.org/bible/1+Chronicles+3
